title: Index Selection, Selectivity, Sequential Scans, and When Indexes Hurt
description: Index Selection, Selectivity, Sequential Scans, and When Indexes Hurt. Interview-first coverage of mechanisms, prediction, diagnosis, and trade-offs.
learningObjectives: Explain selectivity and its effect on access-path cost.
Explain why PostgreSQL may choose sequential scan despite an index.
Compare index, bitmap heap, and sequential scans.
Identify index write, storage, cache, vacuum, and operational costs.
Use workload evidence to justify adding or removing indexes.

mentalModel.text: An index is an option, not an instruction. If a query needs five rows from a million, an index can save a lot of work. If it needs half the table, finding rows through an index and then jumping around the table may cost more than reading the table in order. PostgreSQL estimates those costs and chooses the path it expects to be cheapest.

blocks.text: Selectivity describes the fraction of rows that match a condition. Cardinality is the number of matching rows, estimated by the planner or observed during execution.

Selectivity tells you how much of the table matches a condition. Searching for one rare email is highly selective; searching for a status shared by most orders is not. Cardinality is the actual or estimated number of matching rows.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status='shipped';

blocks.title: Three terms for judging an index
rows: How small a share of rows matches a condition.
One rare email is highly selective; a status held by 70% of orders is not.
How many rows match, estimated by the planner or observed in execution.
The planner expects 100 rows but the query actually returns 40,000.
The method used to find those rows.
An index scan can help for a few rows; a sequential scan can win for a broad result.

blocks.problem: A million-row orders table has a rare external reference and a status column where 70% of rows are 'paid'.
reasoning: A unique reference matches about one row, so it is highly selective.
The status predicate matches roughly 700,000 rows, so using an index may require fetching a large part of the table.
Compare estimated rows with actual rows because bad estimates can lead the planner to choose a poor path.
blocks.outcome: The same index type can be useful for a selective predicate and unhelpful for a broad one.

blocks.text: PostgreSQL can read table pages in order, follow an index to row locations, or use a bitmap to group row locations by page.

A sequential scan reads table pages in order and checks each row. An index scan finds matching keys and then fetches their table rows, which can involve many scattered reads. A bitmap heap scan collects row locations by page to reduce random visits, but usually cannot preserve the index's ordering.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id,total_amount FROM orders WHERE status='shipped';

steps.title: Identify query shape
steps.description: Write down predicates, joins, ordering, limit, and selected columns.

steps.title: Predict the mechanism
steps.description: Explain which pages, entries, or operators the database is likely to visit.

steps.title: Validate the plan
steps.description: Use actual rows and buffers to compare prediction with observed work.

blocks.problem: A query matches 30,000 orders spread across a large table.
reasoning: An index scan may jump to individual row locations, which can mean many scattered page visits.
A bitmap heap scan groups locations by page to reduce repeated random access.
A sequential scan may still win if most table pages are needed; a bitmap path generally does not preserve index order.
blocks.outcome: The planner chooses an access path based on estimated work, not a rule that index scans are always faster.

reasoning: A plain index scan may visit many scattered heap pages to fetch the matching rows.
A bitmap heap scan can group matching row locations by page, reducing repeated random visits, but it still may need a separate sort.
A sequential scan may be cheaper if much of the table is needed. If the query returns only a few rows, a selective index path may win instead.
blocks.outcome: The planner compares the work to find rows, fetch their columns, and produce the requested order. Matching a predicate is only one part of query cost.
blocks.problem: A report returns 35% of orders matching a status and sorts them by total amount.

blocks.text: A sequential scan can be cheapest when the table is small or the query needs a large fraction of its rows.

A sequential scan can be the right choice for a small table or a query that needs many rows. Following an index and then fetching most rows one by one may cost more than reading the table pages together. An index existing does not mean PostgreSQL should use it.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL example
blocks.source: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled';

blocks.problem: An index exists on orders.status, but a report returns 90% of all orders.
reasoning: Using the index can require reading many index entries and then fetching most table rows.
A sequential scan reads table pages in order and checks their rows in one pass.
The exact crossover depends on table size, cache, statistics, and the query.
blocks.outcome: An existing index is an option, not an instruction. A sequential scan can be the sensible choice.

blocks.text: Every index speeds some reads but creates ongoing work for relevant writes, storage, memory, and maintenance.

Every index must be updated when relevant rows change. Indexes use disk and memory, add work to writes and WAL, and need maintenance as rows are deleted or updated. Keeping unused indexes can slow the whole workload, not just take up space.

blocks.prompt: Does the existence of an index guarantee PostgreSQL will use it?
blocks.explanation: The planner compares estimated costs, and another access path may be cheaper.

blocks.problem: A high-write events table has eight indexes, but only three support frequent queries.
reasoning: Each insert must maintain relevant indexes; updates can also change index entries.
Extra indexes consume disk and cache space and can increase WAL and maintenance work.
Use workload evidence to identify unused or duplicate indexes before considering removal.
blocks.outcome: Evaluate indexes against the whole workload: read benefit, write cost, storage, and maintenance.

blocks.text: For example, adding five indexes to a write-heavy orders table means every insert must maintain five extra lookup structures where applicable. That can increase write latency, WAL volume, cache pressure, and storage. Before keeping an index, compare how often it helps important reads with the ongoing cost imposed on writes.

blocks.title: Inventory index size, usage, and validity
blocks.source:
SELECT s.schemaname,
       s.relname AS table_name,
       s.indexrelname,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid)) AS index_size,
       s.idx_scan,
       i.indisvalid,
       i.indisready,
       i.indisprimary,
       i.indisunique
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes AS s
JOIN pg_index AS i ON i.indexrelid = s.indexrelid
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid) DESC;

blocks.title: Optional B-tree health details with pgstattuple

blocks.text: `pg_relation_size` tells you how many bytes an index occupies; it does not prove the index is bloated. `pgstatindex` can report B-tree structure details such as leaf density and fragmentation, but it scans the index and can consume I/O, so schedule it thoughtfully on large production indexes. There is no single bloat percentage that proves an index should be rebuilt: compare size, page density, workload, query plans, maintenance history, and the cost of rebuilding.
Measure before adding or dropping an index, and change one thing at a time so you can tell what caused the result.

Before adding or dropping an index, look at real query frequency, latency, plans, write rate, and index size over a representative period. Change one thing at a time and check whether the improvement to reads is worth the extra write and storage cost.

blocks.problem: A dashboard query is slow, and the team proposes an index on every column in its WHERE clause.
reasoning: Capture the exact query, representative parameters, frequency, and current plan.
Check whether the bottleneck is scanning, repeated joins, sorting, or returning many rows.
Test one candidate index, compare latency and buffer activity, and measure write overhead.
blocks.outcome: An index is justified by a measured workload improvement, not merely because a column appears in WHERE.

steps.title: Capture a baseline
steps.description: Record query latency, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) where safe, index size, write latency, and representative workload timing.

steps.title: Verify usage and dependencies
steps.description: Review idx_scan across at least one normal workload cycle, when statistics were last reset, query logs/plans, UNIQUE/PRIMARY KEY constraints, foreign-key needs, and overlapping indexes.

steps.title: Build the replacement
steps.description: If needed, use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY outside an explicit transaction block, while monitoring write load and replica lag.

steps.title: Verify before removing the old index
steps.description: Check pg_index.indisvalid and indisready, compare plans and latency, and let the changed workload run through peak and low periods.

steps.title: Remove cautiously
steps.description: Drop only a confirmed unneeded, non-constraint-backed index with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY; monitor for regressions and retain a recreate/rollback plan.

blocks.title: Check whether a concurrent index build is valid
blocks.source:
SELECT idx.oid::regclass AS index_name,
       pi.indisvalid,
       pi.indisready,
       pi.indisunique
FROM pg_class AS idx
JOIN pg_index AS pi ON pi.indexrelid = idx.oid
WHERE idx.oid = 'public.idx_orders_customer_created'::regclass;

blocks.title: Check in-progress index builds
blocks.source:
SELECT pid, command, phase,
       lockers_total, lockers_done,
       blocks_total, blocks_done,
       tuples_total, tuples_done
FROM pg_stat_progress_create_index;

blocks.text: Never drop an index only because `idx_scan = 0`: statistics may have been reset, the workload window may omit rare jobs, or the index may support a constraint. A failed `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` can leave an invalid index and the failure mode depends on whether it is unique and which build phase failed. Inspect `indisvalid`/`indisready`, check logs and duplicate data, then deliberately decide whether to drop and retry. A failed concurrent unique build can still enforce uniqueness after some failures; treat cleanup as a verified operation, not a blanket instruction.
1. Problem and motivation — An email lookup returns one row from ten million, while a status filter returns eight million. An index is not automatically the cheapest plan for both queries.

2. Definition and design choice — Selectivity is the fraction of rows matching a predicate; cardinality is a row count. PostgreSQL estimates sequential, index, and bitmap paths using statistics, page costs, and expected rows.

steps.description: Selectivity describes the fraction of rows that match a condition. Cardinality is the number of matching rows, estimated by the planner or observed during execution.

steps.title: Sequential, index, and bitmap paths
steps.description: PostgreSQL can read table pages in order, follow an index to row locations, or use a bitmap to group row locations by page.

steps.title: Why sequential scan can win
steps.description: A sequential scan can be cheapest when the table is small or the query needs a large fraction of its rows.

steps.title: Indexes cost more than disk
steps.description: Every index speeds some reads but creates ongoing work for relevant writes, storage, memory, and maintenance.

blocks.problem: A 10-million-row table has an email index and a status index. Email matches one row; `status = 'active'` matches eight million rows scattered across the table.
reasoning: For the email lookup, the index can avoid reading most table pages. For the broad status query, millions of scattered heap fetches can cost more than a sequential scan.
A bitmap heap scan can group matching tuple locations by heap page for intermediate result sizes; it is not universally best either.
Each index uses disk and cache space and adds write maintenance. An index can improve one endpoint while making inserts and updates slower.
blocks.outcome: Compare representative plans, actual rows, buffers, and write throughput. Do not force an index because it exists or use one selectivity percentage as a universal cutoff.

blocks.title: 5. Anti-pattern to avoid
blocks.content: More indexes is not automatically better: an index may speed one query while slowing writes and consuming cache.

blocks.prompt: 6. Interview probe — What does high selectivity mean?
blocks.answer: A selective predicate narrows results substantially.
blocks.explanation: A strong answer connects the problem to the mechanism, states assumptions and trade-offs, and explains how to verify the decision in practice.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Trade-off 1
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: More indexes is not automatically better: an index may speed one query while slowing writes and consuming cache.

revisionSheet.text: Selectivity and estimated row count influence path costs.
Sequential scans can be best for small tables or broad predicates.
Bitmap heap scans group heap access but generally do not preserve index order.
Every index adds storage, write, WAL, cache, and maintenance cost.
Use representative plans and workload evidence before adding or dropping an index.

options.text: A predicate matches a small fraction of rows
A predicate matches almost every row
The table has many columns
The index is physically large

questions.explanation: A selective predicate narrows results substantially.

questions.prompt: Why can sequential scan beat index scan when most rows match?

options.text: Sequential page reads can beat many scattered heap fetches
Indexes cannot return many rows
PostgreSQL never uses indexes on large tables
Sequential scans bypass MVCC

questions.explanation: Broad results can make index navigation plus heap access more costly.

questions.prompt: What does a bitmap heap scan do?

options.text: Collects tuple locations and groups heap visits by page
Sorts the table permanently
Stores results in a B-tree
Guarantees index order

questions.explanation: Bitmap scans can reduce random visits but generally do not preserve order.

questions.prompt: Why is there no universal selectivity threshold for index use?

options.text: Cost depends on size, row width, cache, correlation, estimates, and query shape
PostgreSQL ignores statistics
All indexes have equal cost
Sequential scans are prohibited

questions.explanation: The crossover depends on workload and physical costs.

questions.prompt: What is a common cost of another index on a write-heavy table?

options.text: More index maintenance, storage, and cache use
All reads become slower by definition
The table loses its primary key
The index prevents vacuum

questions.explanation: Indexes trade read benefit for write, storage, and maintenance cost.

questions.prompt: A production team needs to replace an index on a busy table. Which approach best limits write blocking?

options.text: Build the replacement with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, verify validity and plans, then remove the old non-constraint-backed index concurrently
Drop the old index first and hope the query remains fast
Run CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY inside a transaction block
Create an index on every column in the table

questions.explanation: A staged concurrent build keeps ordinary writes available during much of the build. Verify the result and workload before removing the old index.

questions.prompt: A 900 MB B-tree index is large. Which conclusion is justified by `pg_relation_size` alone?

options.text: It occupies about 900 MB on disk; this alone does not prove bloat
Exactly 900 MB is wasted space
The index should be dropped immediately
The cache holds the entire index in RAM

questions.explanation: Relation size reports on-disk size, not the portion that could be reclaimed. Diagnose bloat and value using more evidence.

questions.prompt: `idx_scan = 0` for an index in the current statistics view. What should you check before considering removal?

options.text: Stats reset time, a representative workload window, dependencies/constraints, and query plans
Only whether the index name looks old
Whether the database has a replica
Whether all queries use SELECT *

questions.explanation: Zero observed scans can reflect a statistics reset or workloads that run infrequently. Constraint-backed indexes require special care.

questions.prompt: Which can make sequential scan rational?

options.text: Small table
Predicate matches a large fraction
Index path requires scattered heap fetches
An index exists, therefore it must be used

questions.explanation: The planner chooses by cost; index existence alone is not decisive.

questions.prompt: What to consider before dropping a low-usage index?

options.text: Stats reset window and workload seasonality
Constraints and rare critical queries
Storage and write cost
Only idx_scan from the last minute

questions.explanation: Usage counters need context and must be balanced against cost and importance.

questions.prompt: PostgreSQL is always wrong when it chooses a sequential scan while an index exists.
questions.explanation: Sequential scans can be cheaper for small tables or broad predicates.

questions.prompt: A failed concurrent unique-index build can still enforce uniqueness in some failure states, even while the index is marked invalid.
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL documents failure states where an invalid index left by CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY continues to enforce uniqueness. Inspect the build phase, logs, and catalog flags before cleanup.

interviewScenarios.prompt: An interviewer says: “The table has an index, but PostgreSQL uses a sequential scan. The planner is broken.” Respond.
strongAnswerPoints: Explain broad-result and random heap-fetch trade-offs.
Compare estimates to actual rows and inspect buffers.
Check size, row width, correlation, cache, and query shape.
pitfalls: Assuming an index or plan node is automatically good or bad without workload evidence.
Changing multiple variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: Index presence does not make an index path cheapest. For broad predicates, sequential reads can beat scattered heap visits. Capture EXPLAIN ANALYZE with buffers, compare estimates with actuals, and inspect distribution and query shape before concluding the planner is wrong.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A write-heavy table has 40 indexes and disk usage is high. How rationalize the set?
strongAnswerPoints: Map indexes to queries and constraints.
Review sizes, usage over a representative window, plans, and overlapping prefixes.
Test reversible changes and monitor reads, writes, WAL, vacuum, and latency.
pitfalls: Assuming an index or plan node is automatically good or bad without workload evidence.
Changing multiple variables before measuring the effect.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: Map each index to queries and constraints, then balance read benefit against storage, cache, write amplification, WAL, and maintenance. Counters alone are insufficient. Test changes in stages and monitor read SLOs and write behavior.
